ex: I bet you thought you were Kwai Chang Caine, didn’t you?
I-I thought it was like she’d think, “Jesus Christ, I’ve never, I’ve never met anyone like him.”
And she- I remember the one time she accidentally walked in she went, “Oh! Oh, sorry. Wrong room.” and left again.

q: Steve signed an Office DVD for a bloke working the till at HMV and asked if it was selling well. What was the reply?
a: Yes, though they'd had a lot of returns from people who didn't like it
x: Yes, mostly to people buying it as a joke present
Not really, the Kumars DVD was outselling it
Only since they'd put it in the bargain bin
f: Ricky imagined the returners not even wanting their money back. Steve: "They really didn't want it in the house."
ex: There was nothing- there was nothing going on. But there was a guy who was in HMV and he was working with a till- been working with a till and he saw me, he said, "Will you sign this DVD?", I went, "Ah, no problem", he- and I said- I was…
I said, "Well, don't tell me that! I don't need to know that!"
What did he- what did he mean? That they didn't like it or that the--
And I said- I said, "What? People have been bringing them back?"--
He said, "They've been bringing them back", I said, "What was the problem?", he said, "They didn't really like it".

q: Steve keeps overhearing strangers slag off The Office. What extra reason did he admit to?
a: He hangs around Office DVD stacks in a T-shirt with him and Ricky on it
x: He follows people out of HMV to listen in
He eats in the same restaurant every night
He wears a fake moustache so nobody notices him
f: One record-shop browser said "I think it's s***" and his mate went "I agree". Ricky: "Maybe everyone's always slagging it off."
ex: That's partly it but also because I keep stand- hanging out by stacks of Office DVDs.
(Laughing) Wearing a t-shirt with a picture of you and me on it.

q: Karl said he'd come in specially on his days off to sort out the prizes. Where did Steve suggest he'd actually got them?
a: By rifling through the drawers up at Capital Gold
x: From the lost property box at reception
f: Karl's reply: "Yeh. Yeah." He said he'd only had three days off because he'd been "workin' all over Christmas".
ex: You've got a nice load of prizes there--
That I've sorted out. I had to come in here especially to sort that out.
Did you rifle through the drawers up at Capital Gold instead of down here?
Yeh. Yeah. Uhh, "Rockbusters" - we're still doin' that.

q: On a family holiday in France when Steve was about fourteen, what left him not knowing where to look?
a: His mate's mum took her top off
x: His sister got changed on the beach
f: Steve's dad "was having none of it". Steve to his mate: "there's your mom with her knockers out, really."
ex: And, obviously, my dad was having none of it. Like, a bit like Karl and obviously my mum wasn’t up for that as I am.
But the person we went with, the mother of the person we went with, she, uh, she took her top off. And I was like, I was- I- didn’t, I-I didn’t know where to look.

Cause I didn’t want to make an issue of it. I didn’t want to make, you know, I didn’t want to- But it was like- cause I was with my mate. I was going, “Well, I’m not sure what to say, but there’s your mom with her knockers out, really.”
“I mean.. that’s your, that’s your mum over there.”

q: Steve said he partied last night like it was 1999. How exactly?
a: On his own, in his flat, crying
x: Down the pub with Karl and Suzanne
At a karaoke bar in Soho
f: Ricky: "Just like 1999." Steve had actually been to see Prince at the Hammersmith Apollo.
ex: Um, Rick, uh- oh, I partied till it was, I partied last night, Rick, like it was 1999.
What, sort of a old-fashioned, sort of, way. Some old records.

q: Steve pictured Karl ringing a newsreader to report insects falling from the sky. Which newsreader?
a: Trevor McDonald
f: In Steve's version Karl begs, "Put it on the news, quick!" and then spots the bird: "Oh, there was a bird, sorry Trev!"
ex: I love the idea, he's straight on the phone to Trevor McDonald "Look, Trevor, there's this caterpillars, insects falling out the sky! They're pulling out the sky now! Put it on the news, quick!" "You sure that wasn't a bird?" "Oh, there…

q: Ricky lay awake aged six wondering where the universe ended. What did Steve imagine young Karl lying awake wondering?
a: Where does Manchester end?
x: Where does the moon go in the day?
Why do buses come in threes?
f: Steve as young Karl: "I assume it goes on forever!" Karl had already said no, he never lay awake wondering about the universe.
ex: Did you ever used to lie awake at night thinking where did the universe end?
I did that when I was about six
Or seven for about a year. When I— when someone said it was...
He was lying awake at night thinking "where does Manchester end?"

q: Ricky wanted a doctor sitting in the corner of the studio to answer Karl's questions. Which doctor did Steve ask was still available?
a: Dr. Fox
f: Ricky's wishlist also had a vet or naturalist, and "a physicist or something, or an astronomer." Karl: "I'd love that."
ex: I don't know how many there are now. I was thinking what we should do on the show as well is have a doctor. To just sit in the corner.
Right. Is this because you're worried about your health?
No, no. Just someone when Karl says "Why are your bollocks there?" The doctor can now go. "Well, let's ask Doctor". And he goes, "They're there because..." And we need a vet as well.

q: Steve wrote down the real name of the Bristol street he grew up on, refusing to say it on air. What did Ricky say worried him about it?
a: The apostrophe-s
x: That it was twinned with Paris
That it had a hyphen in it
f: Ricky: "Because that's blatant!" Steve said it's in the Bristol A-Z and he still spells it out instantly on the phone to disguise it.
ex: But listen, do you know what worries me, it’s the apostrophe-s!
So if I look that up, in the Bristol...
You will find that in the Bristol A-Z. I swear to God.

q: Karl's new charity said it gives people money to buy hammers. What did Steve joke they actually hand out?
a: A gift voucher for B&Q
f: Karl said the charity was "called Care of the World or something" and they were "giving them money to buy hammers".
ex: I was saying, you know, why have I got to give you me bank details? This is the thing. And I was saying to her, I'm sure you'd make more money, right, if you just had the little thing that you put money in. I said, I want to help you out…
They don't give them money! What do you think of these people- Just like these drought planes.
There's a gift voucher for B&Q. So they have to buy a hammer.
They go with the buckets and go and they throw it up and they go "bundle!"

q: Steve's dad asked his mum for a warm winter overcoat for Christmas. What did Steve's grandmother whisper back?
a: Don't worry, his father will be dead soon so he can have his
x: Get one off the market for a fiver
f: That was about twenty years ago. "I'll be honest with you, my father's still waiting." Good news for Grandad, "less good news for my dad".
ex: They- they- exactly, they've basically stayed in bed and, uhh, it was one Christmas when, um, my grandmother said to my dad, uh, "What would you like for Christmas? What do you fancy for Christmas?", and, uhh, this must of been... I don't…
Which is good news. Good news for my grandfather, less good news for my dad--
He phones up, "How is he today?", "He's fine.", he goes, "Okay. Aw, I'm freezin'."

q: Steve said Karl talks about his childhood as if he was born in the thirties. What did he say Karl seemed to take to school?
a: A baked potato
f: Steve also reckoned young Karl "got a hoop with a stick as a Christmas gift."
ex: It is ver- it's such a weird mindset, that. I think it's- that, to me, is what sums up people from that older generation - the forties and fifties. And it seems to me that you've got that kind of mindset. It's like you were born in the…
I th- well I th- no, but I th--
And got a hoop with a stick as a Christmas gift.

q: When Steve was a gangly youngster, what did his grandmother keep telling him?
a: "You'll fill out!"
f: She fed him endlessly to get him there. Ricky: "Yeah. It worked with me though."
s: The Ricky Gervais Guide to The Future · 2009
ex: I was always slightly more handsome in the future.

Like I kept imagine I would grow a little more handsome. People get so-- My grandmother kept telling me "You'll fill out! When you fill out a bit..." She was obsessed with me filling out. This is why she would feed me endlessly, the idea…
Yeah. It worked with me though.
Yeah, you just... really filled out.

q: Dickie Anderson's email listed the show's "comedy characters". Which name on the list made Steve break off to protest "I'm not a character"?
a: Stephen Merchant
f: The list ran "Camp David, Harry Fook... Stephen Merchant" before Steve objected, and Ricky laughed uproariously.
ex: -offering the biggest load of tat as competition prizes, saying 'hairy Chinese kid' 48 times every show, Rockbusters, not bothering to turn up for weeks on end, only having three listeners, introducing the comedy characters Camp David…

q: Ricky wondered if Dickie Anderson, who'd typed such an articulate rant, might come and work as their PA. What was Steve's verdict?
a: He can't be any worse than what they've already got
x: He'd need a crash course in Rockbusters
He'd have to sign a gagging order
He'd only last a week with Karl
f: Steve: "Well he can't be any worse than what we've already got." Ricky liked Dickie because he "thinks I'm, you know, a genius".
ex: Erm, but eh, I like the fact that Dickie Anderson had that wonderful rant-I mean it was an articulate email, it was quite long, and he must have typed it immediately. I'm thinking, because he's a fan of the show and he-he thinks I'm, you…
D'you reckon he'd come and work for us?
Erm, well he can't be any worse than what we've already got.

q: Steve cuts through Chinatown on his way to Xfm and insists it isn't a town at all. What is it, at best, according to Steve?
a: A novelty street
f: Ricky agreed: "Gerrard Street does not a town make." Steve: "You've had this little street for about a hundred years... It's not expanding."
ex: This is not... at best, what you’ve got here, is a novelty street.
Yeah. Gerrard Street does not a town make.
No! It’s not a town. You’ve had this little street for about a hundred years.
Just cos you’ve got a little pagoda.
You can’t just call it Chinatown, and claim it’s a town.

q: Ricky vowed to sound more articulate after hearing himself on an old show. How long did Steve reckon the effort would last?
a: About three records
f: Ricky then fumbled a sentence straight away: "Did it then, you see?" Steve: "I don't know quite what that sentence meant."
ex: So I’m really going to make an effort for the listener.
Yeah. It’s not going to happen, is it? You’re going to give up after about three records.
But I thought you were joking. And I thought it was like, “Oh, he’s taking the”- there. Did it then, you see?
Again. I don’t know quite what that sentence meant.

q: Steve hyped the star prize, a widescreen DVD of Stephen King's 'Children Of The Corn'. Who did he remind everyone was its star?
a: Peter Horton
f: "Lest we forget it's got Peter Horton as the star." Steve later reckoned the emails were flooding in for this DVD, not for Karl's competition.
ex: The big one; the big star prize that you’re all playing for is of course the DVD widescreen edition of ‘Children Of The Corn’, Stephen King’s horror film, lest we forget it’s got Peter Horton as the star.

q: According to Steve, what does Children in Need turn the whole country and BBC1 into for one day?
a: One big school fete
f: "It's the worst thing ever." Steve also called the entertainment "ill thought out".
ex: "Children in Need" last night, Rick. Ho-ho!
Ohh. I got - watched a bit of it.
Did you watch any of it, Karl. It's awful isn't it?
It's the worst thing ever, I mean it just -- I've said this before, the thing about "Children in Need", it makes the whole country and BBC1 for one day into just one big school fete.
D’y’know what I mean. It's so pathetic. The entertainment is ill thought out, it's just, it’s just boring --

q: After a caller brought up the Ugly Duckling, Steve said the story got him through bleak nights as a child. Why?
a: He was still waiting to turn into a swan
x: He liked that the duckling found a mum
He was scared of the farmyard bullies
His nan read it in funny voices
f: Ricky: "You couldn't wait to one day turn into a swan." Steve: "Still waiting for it."
ex: "Beautiful Ones". Fella just phoned up and said "You were talking about water fowl before”. Um,

The only – yeah, the only, bird with a penis is the swan, and he said we'd worried him about the ugly duckling, about, oh he turned into a swan, but a ducklings, they’re not called, um, ducklings, they’re called cygnets. I pointed out that…
A duckling, and that’s that - all the other ducks sorta laughed at him 'cause he was all gangly and everything, then he turned into a swan and he realised "Oh, I was a swan all along..."
Yeah, the ugly duckling story got me through so many bleak nights as a child.

q: Driving to Blackpool, Steve heard a BBC DJ say "I seem to have run out of words" live on Comic Relief night. Who did the DJ hope could help?
a: Steve Baxter, the presenter outside
x: The weatherman in the next studio
A listener on the phone line
f: "I wonder if Steve Baxter's got any for me." Steve Baxter, clearly not ready, just went: "Do what – mate?"
ex: And uh, I think this was maybe like sort of, I dunno, BBC Solihull or something, and uh- they've always got like, they've got this, this one guy in the studio doing all the DJing, and um there's some bloke who's sort of outside the BBC…
I love the fact that you remember the man's name.

Well it's important because, er, we were listening and the guy in the studio he's there and he's chatting away, going "Got a signed picture here of er, the Spice Girls, all the girls have signed that, and so the highest bidder gets to win…
He just said, "I seem to have run out of words”. And we were like listening like ... OK ... And he just went, "I seem to have run out of words … I wonder if Steve Baxter's got any for me”.
And Steve Baxter's just outside like obviously not, not ready, just going, “Do what – mate?”

q: A paper ran a photo of a five-year-old girl on the Queen Mother's funeral route, said to be weeping for her. What did Steve reckon?
a: She was just tired and bored
x: She'd lost her balloon in the crowd
Her dad had trodden on her foot
She had something in her eye
f: Steve: "She's just tired and bored and it's so transparent that it's not crying."
ex: Well there’s a picture in the paper today of various people who were lining the pre umm you know the funeral kind of route yesterday and there’s a picture of a very young child maybe sort of five or six on the arms of her dad and her head…
Well she doesn't know, why would she cry?
She’s just tired and bored and it’s so transparent that it’s not crying.

q: What did Steve find 'weird' about Karl's 'facts' compared with the wind-up stories he and Ricky had told Karl?
a: Their made-up stories were more plausible
x: Theirs had come true by accident
f: Steve: "He's willing to believe that a woman's hair fell out when her husband came home and said, 'Let's get married, then'." Ricky: "I think we tried too hard."
ex: The stories that we made up are more plausible--
Than the "facts" he's actually giving us.
Yeah, I think we tried too hard.
That's what he's willing to believe. He's willing to believe that a woman's hair fell out when her husband came home and said, "Let's get married, then".

q: Karl said the old woman downstairs is always sat reading a book every night. What did Steve suggest?
a: That she might be dead
x: That she was spying on Karl
That she'd written the book herself
That she was reading Karl's Diary
f: "Are you sure she's not dead? ... The pages never turn, she never seems to finish it!" Then: "Her cats are dead around her!"
ex: Are you sure she's not dead?
Every time you look down there, she's just flicking through the- she's just reading this book! The pages never turn, she never seems to finish it!
She never moves from her chair!
Are you sur- are you sure the Chinese girl's goin-
Her cats are dead around her!

q: Steve admitted to a phase where he wore a bow tie for about six months. Why?
a: He thought it made him look like he was from a Jeeves and Wooster book
x: His mum said it made him look taller
He was trying to look like a magician
He thought it would help him get into university
f: Steve, for new listeners: "I thought I was very urbane and sophisticated."
ex: Is this before or after the phase when you thought a bow tie would sort you out?
This was before the bow tie phase.
There was a phase, I should say, for new listeners, where I, for about six months wore a bow tie because I thought it made me look sort of like I was from a "Jeeves and Worcester" book.

And I thought I was very urbane and sophisticated. But, yeah, we're doing the school play and there was one point where everyone was hanging out in one of the rooms, music rooms, getting changed, joking, laughing, cracking onto each other…

q: Steve named his disco after the TV show Fantasy Island. What did he insist the show was really about?
a: Love, on an island
x: Plane crashes on a desert island
A millionaire hiding from the taxman
f: Steve: "It was much more a spiritual and emotional journey." He reckoned Ricky had only ever seen the trailer.
ex: 'Cuz everyone up to you looked like Tattoo?
Partly that. And I--'cuz I liked the program Fantasy Island.
Why did you like the program Fantasy Island?
Well, it was about love, on an island.

q: While Steve was DJing to a thousand scouts in a marquee at a jamboree, which song did he put on that sent them wild?
a: Smells Like Teen Spirit
f: Steve: "They were moshing, they were climbing up the poles. The organisers were going, 'Switch that off! Switch that off!'"
ex: Right, and I'll tell you this, we were playin' our stuff. They were lovin' it. They were dancing, it was in a big marquee, right?
I slapped on Smells Like Teen Spirit.

They went mad for it. They were moshing, they were climbing up the poles. The organisers were going, "Switch that off! Switch that off!" Right? They're going crazy, and I was there going, "No! That's what they like. I'm going to do it."…

q: What was Steve's answer to Karl's worry about how you ever put a snake down without it turning on you?
a: You never put it down
x: Put it back in the jar
f: Ricky agreed: "that's why that bloke's got you know, 11 or 12, carrying 'em." Then Steve suggested throwing it "really far".
ex: Well, what you do is, you never put it down, Karl.
Yeah, that's why that bloke's got you know, 11 or 12, carrying 'em.
You never put it down. You sling it, who cares.
You just throw it don't you, really far.
That, I don't think you should throw snakes.
